## Longevity banner commemorating the 73rd birthday of Xu Yingkui  
China, Qing dynasty (1644- 1911), 1903 Silk with metallic threads, 304 x 147 cm Gift of Dr Hui Wai Haan HKUT.2004.1923  
These three longevity banners were presented to Xu Yingkui (1830- 1903), the Qing Governor- General of Fujian and Zhejiang, to commemorate his seventieth and seventy- third birthdays. In 1900, when Xu celebrated his seventieth birthday, he was well known in China for concluding the "Mutual Promise of Southeast China" (dangnan haohe) agreement with other provincial governors and high- ranking officials, such as Zhang Zhidong (1827- 1909) and his Kanyi (1830- 1903). This agreement declared the neutrality of Southeast China in the war between the court of Empress Dowager Cixi (1851- 1908) and the Eight- Nation Alliance of foreign powers during the Boer Rebellion (1899- 1901).  
One of the banners depicts Shoulao, the Daoist God of Longevity, and features an inscription stating that it was presented by Wu Songyang (1846- 1916) to Xu on the occasion of his seventy- third birthday. The text reads:  
ganshou guangdi dafy yunshui stantai fui daree qi zhi jin san nongying  
("for the seventy- third birthday of Yunhuai, the Grand Master of Shenlai's Happiness and the Governor General") sanpai sian fujian shiyong dao shuyu wanguang kou zhu ("since wishes from student Wu Songyang, the third- ranking shiyongdao of Fujian")  
Surrounding Shoulao are various embroidered symbols of Longevity, including a peck, several cranes and five bats. The number of bats is significant—as the Chinese characters for bat and fortune are both pronounced fie, they symbolize the "Five Blessings" of longevity, health, wealth, and a virtuous life and natural land. The other two banners feature large golden haos (longevity) characters that were first embroidered with images of various Daoist immortal deities and not a real saint or nun. The colorfully shaded haos around the shao characters were embroidered using a technique called guangchen ("encroaching sun stich"), in which short straight stitches were embroidered layer upon layer, resulting in a shading of colours moving from light to dark. Embroidered silk banners like these were often used to decorate interiors during birthday or wedding banquets, or as wall hangings in temple lecture halls.
